summary: This note is a general overview of the brain as the center of the nervous system in vertebrates and most invertebrates, comparing brain properties across animal species with the greatest attention to vertebrates. It covers brain anatomy and tissue types (neurons and glia), how neurons signal via axons and synapses, the evolution and size scaling of brains, embryonic development, neurotransmitters and electrical activity, energy use, and how brains process sensory input and control movement. The note defers human-specific material and brain disease to a separate human brain article.
one_line: Overview of the brain as the nervous system's control center across animal species, covering structure, neurons, synapses, evolution, development, and function.
key_facts: The brain is an organ that serves as the center of the nervous system in all vertebrate and most invertebrate animals.
In vertebrates, the hypothalamus is the neural control center for all endocrine systems.
The brain is the most energy-consuming organ of the body.
All vertebrate brains can be embryonically divided into three parts: the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon) and hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
In humans, the cerebral cortex contains approximately 14–16 billion neurons, and the estimated number of neurons in the cerebellum is 55–70 billion.
The human brain has been estimated to contain approximately 100 trillion synapses; even the brain of a fruit fly contains several million.
A myelinated axon is wrapped in a fatty insulating sheath of myelin, which serves to greatly increase the speed of signal propagation.
Action potentials travel along axons at speeds of 1–100 meters per second.
For mammals, the relationship between brain volume and body mass essentially follows a power law with an exponent of about 0.75.
Humans have an average encephalization quotient (EQ) in the 7-to-8 range, while most other primates have an EQ in the 2-to-3 range.
Most vertebrate species devote between 2% and 8% of basal metabolism to the brain, while in humans it rises to 20–25%.
The first vertebrates appeared over 500 million years ago, during the Cambrian period, and may have resembled the modern hagfish in form.
Arthropods have a central brain, the supraesophageal ganglion, with three divisions and large optical lobes behind each eye.
Cephalopods such as the octopus and squid have the largest brains of any invertebrates.
Glutamate almost always exerts excitatory effects on target neurons, while gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is almost always inhibitory.
Dale's principle holds that, with few exceptions, each neuron releases the same neurotransmitter or combination of neurotransmitters at all of its synaptic connections.
The blood–brain barrier blocks the passage of many toxins and pathogens, though it also blocks antibodies and some drugs.
In mammals, the cerebral cortex tends to show large slow delta waves during sleep and faster alpha waves when awake but inattentive.

entities.name: hypothalamus
entities.role: small part of the vertebrate brain that is the neural control center for all endocrine systems

entities.name: blood–brain barrier
entities.role: barrier formed by tightly joined blood vessel wall cells that blocks many toxins and pathogens

entities.name: Cryogenian period
entities.role: geological period in which the common ancestor of all bilaterians appeared, 700–650 million years ago

entities.name: raphe nuclei
entities.role: small brainstem area that is the exclusive source of serotonin

entities.name: locus coeruleus
entities.role: small area near the raphe nuclei that is the exclusive source of norepinephrine, involved in arousal

entities.name: Dale's principle
entities.role: rule that each neuron releases the same neurotransmitter(s) at all its synaptic connections

entities.name: cerebral cortex
entities.role: brain part containing roughly 14–16 billion neurons in humans and most strongly distinguishing mammals

entities.name: prefrontal cortex
entities.role: brain area controlling executive functions, planning, working memory, and attention, especially well developed in humans

entities.name: supraesophageal ganglion
entities.role: central brain of arthropods with three divisions and large optical lobes

entities.name: hagfish
entities.role: modern fish form that the first vertebrates may have resembled
